title: We tried a bunch of AI game dev workflows. Here's what we kept.
author: BoldElara92
selftext:
Took a while to find something that actually held up.

First instinct was to automate as much as possible from the start. That backfired pretty fast. Errors stacked on each other and we ended up spending more time fixing AI mistakes than if we'd just done it manually.

What ended up working was keeping planning and execution separate. Think through the logic first, then let AI handle implementation. Sounds obvious in hindsight but it took an embarrassing number of failed attempts to get there.

The other thing nobody really talks about is QA. AI is not as consistent as you'd expect. We had to add a dedicated review pass just to catch stuff that technically worked but felt wrong in the actual game.

Still iterating on it. Curious how others are structuring their process right now.

comments.author: count023
comments.body:
mine is the same. Plan first, usually with a smarter AI like opus, break it all down into discrete pieces. 

Like in my CIvilization like game i'm working on, i did diplomacy, intel, territory control, city structure, unit and combat, all those planned in individual piecs. 

plan how the data will be structured out and how they all interact.

  
Once i have implementation done,  have two more passes before any moving on.

  
I first off have a pass for debugging and testing, obivous and self explanatory to pick up bugs and isues.

  
Then i run a few agents over the top as the code goes on.

First one, "identify any static entries, hardcoded dependencies, magic numbers and lazy inferences that should be isolated".

Second one, "identify any refactor opportunities"

third one: "does this align with the accepted plan and design, is there any suggestions for enhancements or plan review in other phases"

replies.author: BoldElara92
replies.body:
Planning first really does save time. We tried automating everything upfront and just made mistakes faster. With story-driven stuff, bugs hide until you actually play through it, so we do a manual pass early before letting AI do refinements.

When you run those refinement checks, do you review everything at once or break it into sections? Breaking it into pieces catches way more issues for us.

replies.author: count023
replies.body:
I review the code at a high level, as in, does the structure look about right nad do no glaring dependencies or repeated patterns turn up, i dont go line by line if you get my meaning. But even that is more then enough to go, "oi, you have a LUT there you should't have!" or "why is this function global? is it just so this other function can access a variable that should be scoped elsewhere?" and fix the ai up.

And then under review, the AI gives me a list of "what could be refactored/fixed/improved" and "design change suggestions" and i go back ot plan mode to decide what to do wtih all 3 before moving on. 

I review at each gate. So basically if i'm working in a game on say, a diplomacy system, i'd check at milestones periodically and then move on. Milestones would obviously be major changes that might impact performance/appearance, so building a UI or linking into other functions or new gameplay elements, stuff like that which naturally makes sense to test as gates.

comments.author: jimmybobjoeflow
comments.body: The QA thing is so real and I feel like people gloss over it because it's unglamorous. We ended up building a dedicated review layer just for game feel. Stuff that clears every technical check but plays weird in context. Once we treated that as its own production stage rather than a cleanup step, consistency improved a lot. It's extra work upfront but it's the reason our output actually holds up.

replies.author: BoldElara92
replies.body:
This is the insight that changes things. Most people think the review layer is about catching bugs, but you're right that it's its own stage. For narrative games especially, that pass catches pacing issues, tone shifts, branching logic that's technically correct but narratively wrong.

The thing is, it also informs the next round of generation. Like you notice dialogue feels off in a scene, and suddenly you understand what the character needs to sound like. That feedback loops back into what you ask the AI to do next.

comments.author: Yenii_3025
comments.body:
"What ended up working was keeping planning and execution separate. Think through the logic first, then let AI handle implementation. Sounds obvious in hindsight but it took an embarrassing number of failed attempts to get there."

I don't understand what you're saying here. What were you doing instead of planning before executing the plan?

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body: AI is changing so fast.  Fable 5 is ridiculous.  I'm about to try to combine it with Claudius, the plug-in for unreal to let it work in engine.

comments.author: AutomaticTalent
comments.body:
Lots of QA and iterative feedback loops.  It helps that I was a QA manager for a few years but also I'm pretty demanding when it comes to my entertainment software so as I think of things I keep pushing the envelope.

One thing I found interesting, just let the AI make it's slop interface to get you moving through the steps then as things come together and the core game loop is fun you will start to see how to add the icing (more graphics/audio/tuning) and meld the interface together.

replies.author: BoldElara92
replies.body:
Exactly. The iteration layer isn't just polish, it's part of design. Most creators want final visuals before moving on, but early generations actually inform branching and narrative in ways you can't predict. Sometimes the "wrong" outputs are the most useful feedback.

Hard part is knowing when to stop iterating. People who finish games treat each version as "what does this tell me" rather than chasing perfection.

replies.author: AutomaticTalent
replies.body:
Feature Creep - going through it right now.  Are these things necessary?

High score page. - yes.  But I couldn't MAKE one before the game could give me a high score.  Oh, then I want to show it on the game play page so the player can beat it - realized that while playing with a high score table.

I have good sense of what's essential and now I'm balancing the wanna-haves against the release date.  A tale as old as software development for sure - just one more feature....

comments.author: Silly-Party-6484
comments.body:
I get the separation theory but this only works if you actually finish the planning phase. We tried this and ended up spending months planning while the AI could've generated iterations that informed our planning. Sometimes you need to prototype fast and learn from what the AI shows you rather than planning everything upfront.

The QA point is solid though.

comments.author: Elpepestan
comments.body:
Planning first is good but I think the bigger issue is scope. Most people throw way too much at AI at once. We scale up slowly, test each layer before adding the next. That's what actually prevents cascading errors, not just better planning. Planning a massive game then trying to execute it all at once still breaks.

The QA thing though yeah obviously necessary.

comments.author: Deep_Ad1959
comments.body: the plan-first then let-ai-execute split is the part i'd push back on, at least for the prototyping stage you said ai was best at. early on the generating IS the planning. you find the design by watching a rough version play wrong, not by speccing logic upfront. separating the two makes sense once you already know what you're building, but before that the fast iterate loop is how you figure it out, and front-loading a full plan slows down the one thing ai is reliably good at here. the dedicated qa pass i'm with you on completely.

comments.author: Pristine-Collar-9037
comments.body: I think separating planning from implementation is underrated. Once the game rules and constraints are clear, AI seems to produce much more consistent results than when it's asked to invent everything on the fly
